headline: At 0.1 Hertz: Breathing Science and Its Mystical Overhang
lede: Breathing slowly is genuinely good for you: the physiology is settled, the blood-pressure reductions are replicated, and the underlying mechanism — cardiovascular resonance at 0.1 hertz — has been understood since the nineteenth century. Jack Sweeney, the programmer who built bots to track Elon Musk's private jet, is now selling a breathwork app built around these techniques. The tweets promoting it start from real science and end somewhere physiologists have never been.
body:
Breathing at roughly six cycles a minute — five and a half seconds in, five and a half seconds out — does something measurable in cardiovascular physiology. The *baroreflex*, the body's automatic blood-pressure feedback loop, has an inherent oscillation period of about ten seconds, placing its natural resonance near 0.1 hertz. When breathing is paced at that frequency, the resulting fluctuations in heart rate align with the baroreflex's own cycle, producing a large amplification of *heart rate variability* (HRV). The cardiovascular system did not need wellness culture to discover this: the oscillation — called the *Mayer wave*, named for the nineteenth-century Austrian physiologist Sigmund Mayer — was identified in the 1870s. Clinical benefits are real: a 2023 meta-analysis of thirty-one studies found paced slow breathing reduced systolic blood pressure by roughly six millimetres of mercury and cut anxiety scores meaningfully.

The tweet's claim that this breathing "creates a 0.1hz pump wave in your cranial-sacral channel" is where biology departs for pseudoscience. The phrase borrows the language of *craniosacral therapy (CST)*, an alternative-medicine modality developed by osteopath John Upledger in the 1970s, which posits a rhythmic pulse flowing through cerebrospinal fluid between skull and sacrum. A 2024 systematic review of fifteen randomised controlled trials found CST "produces no benefits in any of the musculoskeletal or non-musculoskeletal conditions assessed" and judged its anatomical premise implausible: cranial sutures fuse in adolescence, making the alleged skull-bone movement physically impossible. Cerebrospinal fluid does exhibit low-frequency pulsations near 0.1 hertz, but neuroimaging research attributes these to arterial hemodynamics, not to any discrete anatomical passage. No structure called the cranial-sacral channel appears in standard anatomy.

The claim that pairing slow breathing with "elevated emotions" causes the heart and brain to "sync up" has partial scientific grounding and a large commercial backstory. The HeartMath Institute, a California research organisation founded in 1991, publishes peer-reviewed work on paced breathing increasing *vagal tone* — activity in the parasympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system, associated with calm and recovery. HeartMath defines *heart-brain coherence* as measurable entrainment between HRV rhythms and brain electrical activity during its protocols; this has been observed in EEG studies, though effect sizes are debated and a meaningful portion of the cited research appears in HeartMath's own publications rather than independent journals. The word "aura" — used to describe what Sweeney's techniques build or shape — does not appear in any peer-reviewed physiology. The human body does emit electromagnetic fields detectable by sensitive instruments, but no evidence links breathing exercises to an aura as a buildable energetic envelope.

The accompanying "Vortex Breath" — inhale and exhale intervals descending through the Fibonacci sequence: thirteen seconds, eight, five, three, two, one, then a thirteen-second hold — has no peer-reviewed support whatsoever. The technique appears to originate with Nick Sweeney, Jack's brother and co-founder of the Coherence app; the app's own web page for the technique cites zero academic papers. The biological reality is that the *golden ratio* (approximately 1.618, the mathematical relationship connecting consecutive Fibonacci numbers) does appear in certain anatomical structures — the branching geometry of bronchial airways, patterns in cardiac geometry — but the presence of Fibonacci proportions in anatomical architecture says nothing about whether breathing at Fibonacci time intervals produces any distinct physiological effect. Describing the technique as forming "a caduceus or vortex in your aura" is unfalsifiable; no instrument or experimental framework measures or quantifies an aura.

Sweeney built his public profile by tracking the private jets of Elon Musk, Taylor Swift, and Russian oligarchs using publicly available FAA flight data; he has no documented credentials in physiology or medicine. The Coherence app he co-founded launched in early 2025 and markets itself with statistics attributed to "HeartMath Institute and the Journal of Applied Physiology" without linking to specific papers. The mystical framing — auras, caduceus vortices — appears in his personal social media promotion, not in the app's official materials, which use more cautious scientific language. It is worth noting that the largest randomised controlled trial of coherent breathing to date — four hundred participants, four weeks, published in *Scientific Reports* in 2023 — found no measurable effect over a well-designed breathwork placebo. Both groups improved equally. The real benefit of slow pacing may owe more to the simple act of breathing slowly than to any specific rhythm, a conclusion that would not distinguish Sweeney's app from a kitchen timer.

concepts.definition: The body's automatic blood-pressure regulation system. Sensors in the arteries detect pressure changes and signal the brainstem to adjust heart rate and vessel tone. The feedback loop has an inherent oscillation period of roughly ten seconds, giving the cardiovascular system a natural resonance near 0.1 hertz — the frequency that slow paced breathing targets.

The variation in the time between successive heartbeats. Higher HRV generally indicates a well-functioning autonomic nervous system capable of flexible responses. Slow paced breathing amplifies HRV by synchronising respiratory effort with the baroreflex's natural oscillation cycle.

A spontaneous oscillation of arterial blood pressure at approximately 0.1 hertz in humans, first described by the Austrian physiologist Sigmund Mayer in the 1870s. It arises from the baroreflex feedback loop. During resonance breathing, the respiratory cycle entrains with and amplifies this wave, which is why slow breathing has measurable cardiovascular effects.

An alternative-medicine practice developed by osteopath John Upledger in the 1970s, based on the premise that a rhythmic pulse flows through cerebrospinal fluid between the skull and the sacrum and can be detected and manipulated by trained hands. Mainstream medicine does not support its anatomical premise (cranial sutures fuse in adolescence) or its clinical effectiveness; multiple systematic reviews find no benefit for any condition.

A measure of the activity level of the vagus nerve, the main conduit of the parasympathetic ('rest and digest') branch of the autonomic nervous system. Higher vagal tone is associated with lower resting heart rate, greater HRV, and better stress regulation. Slow breathing reliably increases it by amplifying the baroreflex loop.

A term used by the HeartMath Institute to describe measured entrainment between heart rate variability rhythms and brain electrical activity (EEG) during their paced-breathing and positive-emotion protocols. Independent scientists use 'coherence' more narrowly as a mathematical phase-alignment metric; HeartMath's algorithm is proprietary and its broader claims about the heart transmitting intelligence to the brain are contested outside its own publications.

A mathematical proportion (approximately 1.618, written as phi) produced by dividing a line so the ratio of the whole to the larger segment equals the ratio of the larger segment to the smaller. Consecutive Fibonacci numbers (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13…) approximate this ratio. It appears in some anatomical structures but there is no evidence that mimicking it in breathing intervals produces distinct physiological effects.

The individual breathing rate at which heart rate variability oscillations are maximally amplified, because the respiratory cycle aligns with the baroreflex's natural feedback loop. It falls between about 4.5 and 6.5 breaths per minute in adults — often near 6 bpm (roughly 5 seconds in, 5 out) — though the precise value varies by person and ideally requires calibration rather than a universal default.

fact_check: Three claims are incorrect or unsubstantiated. First, a 'cranial-sacral channel' is not an anatomical structure; the phrase borrows the discredited framework of craniosacral therapy, which systematic reviews find anatomically implausible and clinically ineffective. Second, the Fibonacci-interval 'Vortex Breath' has no peer-reviewed support; the golden ratio's appearance in anatomical geometry does not imply any benefit from breathing at Fibonacci time intervals. Third, 'aura' is not a recognised physiological entity — no instrument or study framework supports the idea that breathing builds or shapes one. Even the well-founded core claim — that breathing at approximately 0.1 hertz amplifies HRV via baroreflex resonance — was not confirmed over placebo in the largest randomised controlled trial on the subject (Scientific Reports, 2023, n=400).
thread_summary: The bookmark is tweet number 2 in a numbered list of self-described tools that Sweeney is promoting, apparently in connection with the Coherence breathwork app he co-founded with his brother Nick. Tweet 1 covers 'Vortex Breath,' a Fibonacci-sequence protocol said to form a 'caduceus in your aura'; tweet 2 covers coherence breathing paired with positive emotion. The series blends genuine slow-breathing physiology with New Age metaphysics in a format characteristic of wellness-influencer content.

sources.title: Mechanisms Contributing to the Generation of Mayer Waves
sources.note: Establishes that Mayer waves arise from baroreflex feedback, not from a craniosacral channel.

sources.title: Is Craniosacral Therapy Effective? Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
sources.note: Healthcare (MDPI) 2024; 15 RCTs reviewed; no evidence for CST's effectiveness or anatomical plausibility.

sources.title: Systematic Review of Craniosacral Therapy: Biological Plausibility, Reliability and Clinical Effectiveness
sources.note: Landmark early review establishing CST's anatomical implausibility; fused cranial sutures preclude the claimed movement.

sources.title: Human CSF Movement Influenced by Vascular Low Frequency Oscillations and Respiration
sources.note: Frontiers in Physiology 2022; CSF does pulsate near 0.1 Hz but through arterial hemodynamics, not a craniosacral channel.

sources.title: Slow-Paced Breathing Meta-Analysis
sources.note: Springer Mindfulness 2023; 31 studies, n=1,133; confirms blood-pressure and anxiety reductions from slow breathing.

sources.title: Effect of Coherent Breathing on Mental Health — Randomised Placebo-Controlled Trial
sources.note: Scientific Reports 2023, n=400; largest RCT on coherent breathing; no effect over placebo after four weeks.
